title: "Async Iterators with Stream"

# Async Iterators with Stream

A `Stream` is an iterator whose next item is a future. You poll it from an async context. The trait used in application code today is `futures::Stream`, not a loop of `Iterator` on a blocking call.

```toml
[dependencies]
futures = "0.3"
```

The examples use `futures::executor::block_on` so they run from `fn main` without a larger runtime. A Tokio program awaits the same streams inside an async function and does not call `block_on` on a runtime thread.

## The concept

`Iterator::next` returns `Option<Item>` now. `Stream::poll_next` returns `Poll<Option<Item>>`. You rarely call `poll_next`. You call `StreamExt::next`, which is async, or `collect`, `map`, `then`.

Adaptors are lazy here too. `map` does not run until the stream is polled.

## Recipe 59 — Creating a Stream from a Vec and consuming it

```rust
fn main() {
    use futures::executor::block_on;
    use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};

    block_on(async {
        let mut numbers = stream::iter(vec![10, 20, 30]);
        assert_eq!(numbers.next().await, Some(10));
        let rest: Vec<_> = numbers.collect().await;
        assert_eq!(rest, [20, 30]);
    });
}
```

`stream::iter` turns an `IntoIterator` into a stream that is always ready. `next` takes `&mut` the stream, so `numbers` is `mut`. `collect` drives it to completion.

## Recipe 60 — Streaming lines from a file

This recipe reads a real file, then yields each line as an item. The read itself is synchronous `std::fs`. The stream starts after the `String` exists. That is the right tool for a small log. It is the wrong tool for a file larger than you want in memory. Line-at-a-time async IO belongs to the runtime (`tokio::io::AsyncBufReadExt::lines` on a Tokio file) and still produces a stream of lines. The consumer below does not change.

```rust
fn main() {
    use futures::executor::block_on;
    use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};
    use std::io::Write;

    let path = std::env::temp_dir().join("iterator-cookbook-lines.txt");
    {
        let mut file = std::fs::File::create(&path).unwrap();
        writeln!(file, "ada").unwrap();
        writeln!(file, "linus").unwrap();
    }
    let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&path).unwrap();
    let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&path);

    let names: Vec<String> = block_on(async {
        stream::iter(text.lines().map(str::to_string).collect::<Vec<_>>())
            .collect()
            .await
    });
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada", "linus"]);
}
```

`text.lines()` borrows `text`. Mapping to `String` before `stream::iter` lets the stream own its items. Building that `Vec<String>` up front is the memory cost called out above.

## Recipe 61 — Consuming a channel as a Stream

`futures::channel::mpsc::Receiver` implements `Stream`. Dropping the sender ends the stream.

```rust
fn main() {
    use futures::channel::mpsc;
    use futures::executor::block_on;
    use futures::stream::StreamExt;
    use futures::SinkExt;

    let (mut tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(4);
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        block_on(async move {
            tx.send("ada").await.unwrap();
            tx.send("linus").await.unwrap();
        });
    });

    let names: Vec<&str> = block_on(rx.collect());
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada", "linus"]);
}
```

The thread sends, then drops `tx` when the async block ends. `collect` on `rx` waits until the channel is closed and returns the items in send order. Buffer size `4` is enough for two names. A full buffer waits inside `send` until the receiver takes an item. If the same thread both filled an unbounded amount of work and refused to poll the receiver, that wait would stall. Here the sender is a different thread.

## Recipe 62 — Transforming a Stream with map() and then()

`map` is synchronous. `then` runs an async closure per item and waits for it before the next item of this stream.

```rust
fn main() {
    use futures::executor::block_on;
    use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};

    let out: Vec<i32> = block_on(async {
        stream::iter(["10", "20"])
            .map(|text| text.parse::<i32>().unwrap())
            .then(|n| async move { n + 1 })
            .collect()
            .await
    });
    assert_eq!(out, [11, 21]);
}
```

Use `map` when the transform does not await. Use `then` when each item starts I/O or another future. `then` on this stream is sequential. It does not start the next future until the current one finishes. Concurrent processing is a buffered adaptor such as `buffered` or `buffer_unordered`, and those add a bound you should set on purpose.

## Recipe 63 — Merging multiple Streams

`futures::stream::select` polls two streams and yields whichever item is ready. It is not a sort. If you need sorted output, sort afterwards, or merge two iterators that are already sorted (the itertools chapter).

```rust
fn main() {
    use futures::executor::block_on;
    use futures::stream::{self, select, StreamExt};

    let mut merged: Vec<i32> = block_on(async {
        let odds = stream::iter(vec![1, 3]);
        let evens = stream::iter(vec![2, 4]);
        select(odds, evens).collect().await
    });
    merged.sort();
    assert_eq!(merged, [1, 2, 3, 4]);
}
```

The sort makes the assert about the set of items, not about which stream `select` happened to poll first. Both are ready immediately, so the poll order is an implementation detail.

## Recipe 64 — Stream vs Iterator: when to use which

Use `Iterator` when the next item is already in memory or behind a blocking call you are willing to make on this thread. Use `Stream` when producing the next item must await: a socket, a timer, an async channel, a spawned task.

Wrapping a `Vec` in `stream::iter` does not make the work asynchronous. Recipe 59 does it only to show the consumer API. In a program that has the `Vec` already, `for` or `iter` is the direct tool.

Do not call blocking `std::fs` or `std::thread::sleep` inside `StreamExt::map` on an async runtime thread. That blocks every task on that worker. The blocking work belongs on `spawn_blocking`, or the API should be async and the stream should `then` it.
